section.title: Overview
section.p: riscos-tooltester is a test runner for command-line tools. A suite is a plain text description of the commands to run, the output and return code each should give, and any files it should create. The runner executes each test, compares the result with what the suite expects, and reports which tests passed, failed or crashed. It is intended for integration testing of the behaviour of a tool as a user sees it, rather than for unit testing.
The runner is a single Perl script, tooltester.pl, which has no dependencies beyond Perl. It is installed under the name riscos-tooltester, and it can also be run with perl tooltester.pl.

This document describes the command line, and then the format of the files that make up a suite. The suite is described in a test script, normally tests.txt, which refers to files of expected output, replacement scripts that normalise output which varies from run to run, and data files that the tests use.

Tests run with the working directory set to test-directory, not the directory riscos-tooltester was started from, so a relative path such as a bare leafname or ./mytool will not resolve unless the tool also happens to live under the test directory; give an absolute path, or a path already resolvable through the PATH environment variable, for a tool that lives elsewhere.

use.p: riscos-tooltester runs a command-line tool repeatedly according to a plain text test description, captures output, checks return codes, and can validate files or directories created by the tool.

The normal calling convention is to place any switches first, then pass the tool under test and the directory containing the suite. By default the runner reads tests.txt from that directory. The script format is designed for repository-local maintenance: it is simple to diff, easy to split with Include:, and keeps expected output in ordinary text files.

Tests are arranged into Group: blocks and Test: entries. A group establishes default statements such as Command:, Replace:, or Env:; each following test inherits those values and may override them or clear them with a leading minus form such as -Expect:.

Captured output is compared against the file named by Expect: after any optional replacement script named by Replace: has normalised unstable data such as paths, timestamps, branch names, or memory addresses. When output mismatches, the runner writes the post-replacement actual output to the expectation pathname with -actual appended, which makes it easy to inspect the real result before updating the expected file.

The tool also checks side effects. Creates: and CreatesDir: assert that files or directories were created, Removes: and Absent: assert that paths are absent after the run, and built-in checker families such as text, binary, aof, alf, and elf can validate the created file content or structure.

Use -group and -test for narrow reruns while debugging. Add -show-command, -show-output, or -show-diff when you need more diagnostics. The -diff-context option restricts displayed diffs to the selected number of unchanged lines around each change; by default all unchanged lines are shown. Use -junitxml when integrating the results with CI reporting.

The standalone -diff-files form compares an expected file with an actual file using the same display as a failed test, without loading tests.txt or running a tool. Both the single-hyphen and double-hyphen spellings are accepted for these long options.

section.title: File format overview
section.p: This chapter describes the plain text file formats used by riscos-tooltester. The runner is intentionally simple: test suites are line-oriented text files, expectations are ordinary text files, and optional replacement scripts normalise unstable output before comparison.

subsection.title: Suite layout and defaults
subsection.p: The normal suite entry point is a file named tests.txt in the chosen test directory, though the runner can be pointed at a different file with -script. A suite directory commonly contains:

item.p: one main script file, usually tests.txt;
expected output files, often under expect/;
replacement scripts used to normalise unstable output before comparison; and
optional input data files, often under testdata/.

subsection.p: The script is read line by line. Blank lines and lines beginning with # are ignored.

subsection.title: Statement syntax
subsection.p: Each statement has one of these forms:

definition-table.definition: Begin a group. The group establishes default statements inherited by later tests in that group.
Begin one individual test. It starts as a copy of the current group settings, then any following statements override or clear those inherited values.

subsection.p: To clear an inherited value from the current group, write the same keyword with a leading minus and no value, such as -Expect: or -Creates:.

subsection.title: Core suite commands
subsection.p: The runner accepts the following built-in suite statements:

definition-table.definition: Read another suite file inline at that point. This is commonly used to split a large suite into smaller files.
Set the suite name used in JUnit XML output. If omitted, the runner infers a name from the script filename where possible.
Command line to execute for the test. The command may contain substitution variables such as $TOOL, $FILE, or $ARGS.
Select which output stream is captured for comparison. The default is both.
Source file value, available to substitutions as $FILE and $BASE.
Arbitrary argument string, available as $ARGS and tokenised into $ARG1, $ARG2, and so on.
Expectation file containing the expected captured output.
Replacement script applied to captured output before comparison.
One or more files that must be created by the command. The runner removes any pre-existing paths before the test and removes successful outputs afterwards.
One or more directories that must be created by the command. These are also removed before and after the test.
Expected file length in bytes for files named by Creates:. When more than one created file is named, they must all match this size.
File that the command is expected to delete. The runner creates an empty placeholder before the test so that removal can be checked.
File that must not exist after the command completes.
Expected return code. The default is 0.
File whose contents are supplied on standard input.
One line of text supplied on standard input, with a trailing newline appended by the runner.
Environment variable set only for this test execution. This statement may be repeated.
Disable the current group or test, recording the given reason in the reported skip result.

subsection.title: Substitution variables
subsection.p: Most statement values may contain substitution variables. The runner expands the following names:

definition-table.definition: Tool path supplied on the riscos-tooltester command line.
Value supplied by the current File: statement.
Object-file path derived from $FILE using RISC OS build-directory conventions.
Assembler-file path derived from $FILE.
C-file path derived from $FILE.
Leaf filename derived from $FILE.
Full argument string from Args:.
Whitespace-tokenised arguments derived from Args:. Missing values expand to an empty string.

subsection.p: Quoted argument text in Args: is preserved when the numbered $ARGn variables are extracted, so embedded spaces can still be treated as one argument.

Only $ARG1 through $ARG9 are ever defined; a tenth or later argument is simply not made available through a numbered variable. Writing $ARG10 in a command does not fall back to $ARG1 followed by a literal 0: the substitution logic greedily matches as many digits as possible when looking for a variable name, so it treats the whole of ARG10 as the candidate name, finds no such variable, and leaves $ARG10 in the command unsubstituted. A test needing a tenth or later argument should pass it through $ARGS instead and split it within the tested command.

subsection.title: Checker commands
subsection.p: Checker statements use the form <checker>:<parameter>: <value>. They attach extra validation rules to the current group or test and are typically used with one file named by Creates:. The runner currently supports the following checker families:

definition-table.definition: Require the sum of all AOF area sizes to match the given value.
Require the library to contain the given number of files.
Expected ELF endianness.
Expected entry address.

Expected ELF object type, checked as a plain numeric comparison against the file's e_type field with no restriction to particular values. The installed script's own comments only mention 1 (relocatable) and 2 (executable), but the standard ELF enumeration's other small values also work: 3 for a shared object and 4 for a core file.
Expected OS/ABI value.
Expected program-header table offset.
Expected section-header table offset.
Expected ELF header size.
Expected ELF flags field.
Expected size of each program-header entry.
Expected number of program-header entries.
Expected size of each section-header entry.
Expected number of section-header entries.
Expected section-name string-table index.
Compare the created file's textual content against the named file.
Apply a replacement script before the textual comparison.

subsubsection.title: Binary checker

definition-table.definition: Compare the created file byte-for-byte against the named file.
Validate specific offsets described by a separate checkfile.
Apply a replacement script before comparing the binary file rendered as text.

subsection.p: The installed runner does not permit checker use with more than one created file in the same test. If you need checker validation for multiple outputs, split them into separate tests.

subsection.title: Replacement script language
subsection.p: Replacement scripts are miniature line-processing programs. They transform the captured output into a stable form before it is compared against the expectation file, which is useful when the tool prints variable data such as absolute paths, timestamps, branch names, or memory addresses.
The replacement file is read line by line:

item.p: blank lines and comment lines beginning with # are ignored;
all other lines are rules made of zero or more conditions followed by one action.

subsubsection.title: Directives
subsubsection.p: The installed runner supports one directive:

definition-table.definition: Read another replacement file inline. Paths are resolved relative to the current replacement file.

subsubsection.title: Conditions
subsubsection.p: Rules may be restricted by line number, by regular-expression match, or by both together.

definition-table.definition: Apply only to line 5.
Apply only to lines 1 through 5.
Apply only to lines 3 through 10.
Apply only to line 10 onwards.
Apply only when the line matches the regular expression.
Negated regular-expression condition: apply only when the line does not match.

subsubsection.p: The installed script also accepts negation on the numeric range condition by adding ! immediately after it. When both a range and a regular-expression condition are present, both must match for the action to run.

subsubsection.title: Actions

definition-table.definition: Replace the first regular-expression match on the line.
Replace all matches on the line.
Case-insensitive single substitution.
Case-insensitive global substitution.
Write the line to the output immediately and continue with the next input line.
Delete the line from the output.
Stop processing and end the output before the current line.

subsubsection.p: If no rule takes an early action and the end of the rule list is reached, the current line is written to the output unchanged.
